column2: Thousands of excellent Apsarases go to the brave one dead in battle; the master takes the merit of the broken who turn back.
For them the fruit of Brahmin-killing is declared at every step; the gods are for the destruction of one who goes, abandoning his companions.
The fruit of the Ashvamedha is declared for the brave who do not turn back. Victory is with the king firm in dharma; equals should fight equals,
elephants and the rest with elephants and the rest; fugitives are not to be killed, nor spectators, nor those who entered, unarmed, or struck;
against the peaceful, the sleep-overcome, the half-crossed in river or forest, in bad weather, one may practice deceitful warfare for destroying the enemy.
Raising arms one should cry out: "The enemies are broken, broken! Friends and great force have arrived; the leader here has fallen;
the commander is killed and the king too is routed." Striking at the front of fleeing warriors is ordained.
Incenses should be given, knower of dharma, and also great bewilderers; banners and a mass of instruments are fear-causing.
Having obtained victory in battle one should worship gods and Brahmins. Jewels gained in war by a minister go to the king;
his women are not to be protected by anyone else, nor others' by him. An enemy released in battle should be protected like a son;
he should not be fought again; one should maintain the country's customs and the like. Then having reached his own city, he should enter the house under a fixed star,
perform worship of the gods and the rest, protect the warriors' families; one should make a distribution to the servants from what is obtained.
The war-initiation has been told to you, certain for the king's victory.
Wives, sons, house, friends, grain, wealth and the rest — this comes to men, great lady, always by your glance.
Health of body, lordship, destruction of the enemy side, happiness are not hard to get for men looked on by you, goddess.
You are the mother of all beings; the god of gods, Hari, the father; by you and Vishnu, mother, this moving and unmoving world is pervaded.
Do not abandon my honor, treasury, storehouse, house, retinue, body and wife, purifier of all;
do not abandon my sons, friends, cattle or ornaments, you who dwell on the breast of Vishnu, my god.
By truth, purity, conduct and other virtues those men are quickly abandoned who are abandoned by you, stainless one.
Looked on by you, men even without qualities are quickly joined with all virtues, conduct and the rest, with family and lordship.
He is praiseworthy, he virtuous, fortunate, of good family, wise, brave, valiant, whom you, goddess, have looked on.
At once all virtues, conduct and the rest, become defective for him from whom you, mother of the world, beloved of Vishnu, turn away.
Even Brahma's tongue cannot describe your virtues. Be pleased, lotus-eyed goddess; never abandon us.
Pushkara said: Thus praised, Shri gave Indra the boon he wished: firmness of kingdom, victory in battle and the rest.
For those who recite and hear her own hymn it gives enjoyment and liberation; therefore a man should always recite and hear the Shri hymn.
One should make gods favorable through servants by good deeds; one wins a friend by sincerity and relatives by courtesy,
wives and servants by love and gifts, other people by courtesy; no blame in others' affairs, maintenance of one's own duty,
compassion toward the wretched, sweet speech everywhere, helpfulness even with life to a constant friend,
embracing one who comes to the house, giving according to ability, forbearance, no pride in one's own prosperity, no envy at others' growth,
speech that does not pain others, following the silence vow, connection with bound relatives, skill among one's own people,
acting suitably — this is the conduct of the great-souled.
Firmness and secrecy of counsel are declared the wealth of ministers. The priest should be skilled in the three Vedas and in the science of punishment;
he should perform peace-rites and nourishing rites ordained in the Atharva Veda; the wise should judge the goodness of those ministers with those who know it.
One should test two qualities, sight and craft; from his own people one should learn his family, position and restraint;
skill in service, knowledge and capacity to retain — one should test the three qualities; boldness and cordiality likewise;
in conversation one should perceive eloquence and truthfulness; energy, influence and endurance of hardship;
steadiness, affection and constancy in adversity one should mark; devotion, friendship and purity one should know from dealings;
from companions, strength, courage, health and conduct; lack of arrogance and fickleness and not speaking of enmities;
one should know directly the goodness and meanness; unseen virtues and conduct are to be inferred from results everywhere.
A country with crops and mines, holy, with mineral wealth, good for cows, with much water, joined with holy districts,
lovely, with elephants and force, with water, land and roads, not dependent on rain — is praised for great prosperity.
With mostly Shudras, craftsmen and merchants, great undertakings, agricultural, strong, affectionate, hating enemies, able to bear hardship, spacious,
filled with people of various countries, righteous, with cattle, strong, with a leader neither foolish nor addicted — such a country is praised.
One should dwell in a city with wide boundary, great moat, high rampart and gates, with the shelter of mountain, river, desert and forest;
a fort with water, grain and wealth, enduring time, great: water-fort, mountain-fort, tree-fort, earth-fort and bow-fort — the six.
A treasury full of desired goods, fit for ancestors, earned by dharma, able to bear expense, is for increase of dharma and the rest.
An army hereditary, obedient, compact, paid its wages, of famed prowess, of the people, skilled, surrounded by omens,
with various weapons, skilled in various battles, filled with various warriors, with lustrated horses and elephants,
accustomed to travel, fatigue, pain and battles, mostly undivided Kshatriyas — that is held the army of the powerful.
One should make a friend of good family, endowed with yoga, knowledge and courage, with great support, sweet-spoken, capable of the future, undivided;
approaching from afar, speech clear in meaning and following the heart, giving after honoring — these are the threefold gathering of friends.
From a friend there is a threefold fruit of union in dharma, desire and wealth. Of friends, the born-of-one's-own, the bound, the one coming by lineage,
and the one who protected from calamities — a friend is to be known as fourfold. Qualities in a friend: truthfulness and the rest, equal pleasure and pain.
I shall tell the conduct of dependents: the servant should serve the king: skill, goodness, firmness, forbearance, endurance of hardship,
contentment, character and energy adorn the dependent. A servant should attend the king at the proper time, by policy.
He should avoid going to another's place, cruelty, arrogance and envy; a servant should not talk in quarrel with a superior;
he should not reveal the master's secrets, vital points or counsel; he should seek livelihood from the attached and abandon an estranged king;
forbidding in what should not be done and urging in what should be — thus in brief is the good conduct of relatives, friends and dependents.
The king should be the livelihood of all beings like a rain-cloud; at the revenue gates he takes wealth for attaining ends.
He should appoint superintendents endowed with effort in all works: agriculture, trade routes, forts, bridges, elephant-catching,
mines, taking of forces, settling the empty — this eightfold group the king of good conduct should maintain.
From outlaws, thieves, townsmen, the king's favorites, and from the king's greed — the subjects' fear is fivefold;
having foreseen this fear, the king should take the tax in time. He should protect the inner, his body, and the outer, the kingdom;
the king should punish with punishments and protect himself from poison; he should never trust wives and sons with regard to enemies.
Mutual help, friendship, and relationship, and gifts — four — and among them the chief are alliances.
The child, the old, one with long illness, one cast out by kin, the foolish, the timid, the greedy, one whose people are greedy,
one whose subjects are disaffected, one excessively attached to sense objects, one with many-minded counsel, a reviler of gods and Brahmins,
one struck by fate, a reviler of fate, one in famine and trouble, one overwhelmed by troubles of the army,
one in his own country with many enemies, one released by time, and one departed from truth and dharma — these are twenty persons.
With these one should not make peace but only wage war. War among men arises by mutual injury.
One desiring his own rise, or being oppressed by another, endowed with place, time and force, should begin war here.
Of kingdom, women, place and country, of knowledge and strength — plunder, pride, conceit and sensual hurt;
obstruction of knowledge, self-power and dharma, and fate itself; for a friend's sake and insult, and the destruction of kin;
cutting off kindness to beings, corruption of the circle, and attachment to a single aim — these are the sources of war.
Rivalry, land-born, woman-born, speech-born, offence-born — enmity is declared fivefold; one should bring it to calm by means.
